must: multiple-stressor interactions under alternative null models

Source: R/must-package.R
must-package.Rd

Whether a combined effect is called additive, synergistic or antagonistic depends on the null model that defines "no interaction" and on the scale on which effects are combined. must makes these choices explicit and separates three questions:

Details

  1. What the design can identify. describe_design() reports missing treatment combinations, cells shared by several contrasts, the replication unit and repeated measures, and which interactions are identifiable, before any model is fitted.

  2. Which model fits the data. fit_responses() fits a generalised linear mixed model to each response and chooses its error distribution by convergence, residual checks and AIC, independently of the null models.

  3. What "non-additive" means. estimate_interactions() tests each combination of stressors against one or more null models with the same criteria, from the predictions of that model or of one fitted with another package: simple addition (the default), multiplicative, dominance, Bliss independence, stress addition and concentration addition. It distinguishes the net deviation of a combination of three or more stressors from its pure highest-order interaction. By default the tests are corrected for small samples; correction = "none" gives the asymptotic procedure of Madge Pimentel et al. (2025). classify_interactions() assigns the directional classes of Piggott et al. (2015), and summary() and plot() give an overview.

suggest_null_models() applies the guidelines of Schäfer & Piggott (2018) to choose the null models, and report_interactions() writes the methods of the analysis and a table of every decision behind it.

References

Madge Pimentel, I., Albini, D., Beermann, A. J., Leese, F., Macaulay, S. J., Matthaei, C. D., Orr, J. A., Piggott, J. J., & Schäfer, R. B. (2025). Hypothesis-driven research on multiple stressors: An analytical framework for stressor interactions. Ecology and Evolution, 15, e71959. doi:10.1002/ece3.71959

Orr, J. A., et al. (2020). Towards a unified study of multiple stressors: Divisions and common goals across research disciplines. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 287, 20200421. doi:10.1098/rspb.2020.0421

Piggott, J. J., Townsend, C. R., & Matthaei, C. D. (2015). Reconceptualizing synergism and antagonism among multiple stressors. Ecology and Evolution, 5(7), 1538–1547. doi:10.1002/ece3.1465

Schäfer, R. B., & Piggott, J. J. (2018). Advancing understanding and prediction in multiple stressor research through a mechanistic basis for null models. Global Change Biology, 24(5), 1817–1826. doi:10.1111/gcb.14073
